strengths: Novel unifying framework connecting data selection to sequential decision-making with original ADP interpretation of existing methods (Theorem 4.1)

Well-designed controlled experiments validating theoretical predictions, particularly RQ2's message passing experiments demonstrating curvature impact

Unfair RQ1 comparison: DynamicProgramming uses exponential 2^n subset evaluations while baselines limited to 1000 retrainings; lacks computational cost analysis of bipartite method vs. baselines

Overstated critique of existing methods: paper criticizes lack of explicit optimization for sequential objective, but Theorem 4.3 proves optimality under linear utilities and RQ2 shows strong performance under low curvature

Limited experimental scope: only 8 small datasets (50-100 training points), single model class (logistic regression), no neural networks or larger-scale evaluation; scalability and generalization unclear

Incomplete bipartite analysis: lacks characterization of conditions when coverage model accurately captures utility structure, provides no failure mode analysis or when practitioners should prefer existing methods
Incremental empirical improvements: Table 1 shows 2-8% gains on most datasets, inconsistent across domains; no analysis of when/why bipartite excels or fails

strengths: Novel theoretical perspective reformulating data selection as a sequential MDP and analyzing existing methods through approximate dynamic programming

Unifying framework showing that Data Shapley, Beta Shapley, and Data Banzhaf can be interpreted as myopic ADP approximations provides valuable conceptual insight
Comprehensive experimental evaluation against 9 baseline methods with controlled experiments validating theoretical predictions about curvature impact

weaknesses: Critical limitation: Experiments conducted on toy-scale datasets (20 training points for RQ1, 50 for RQ3). Limited novelty: MDP reformulation is natural but straightforward; applying standard DP/ADP is conventional; bipartite method is essentially maximum coverage maximization from well-studied submodular optimization literature

Theory-practice gap: Theory assumes perfect utility function U, but practice uses rough bipartite approximation. Theorem G.3 proves optimality under perfect approximation specification, not on true utility; this gap remains unaddressed

Unclear practical benefits: No computational cost analysis or runtime comparisons; unclear whether improvements from bipartite method stem from better selection or simply more model retraining budget; missing sensitivity analysis for Algorithm 2 hyperparameters

Curvature analysis largely formalizes existing empirical observations (Wang et al. 2024b). The (1-c)² bound is expected for greedy algorithms on submodular functions and does not provide surprising theoretical insights

Inconsistent experimental improvements: Table 1 shows bipartite is best on average but improvements often within one standard deviation of baselines; RQ2 uses artificial message passing rather than real data distributions
Incomplete guidance for practitioners: Paper does not clearly state when to use proposed method versus existing approaches, how to set hyperparameters, or how results scale beyond 100 training points
